speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman (Mr. R. L. Borden) has put that question three or four times, and the answer is an easy one. The government in making this amended contract had no more information and no less than we had when we made the original contract, but the Grand Trunk Railway naturally, on account of the financial changes, which have taken place in the market are a little more timid this year than last. We placed before the House last year all the information we had and the reasons which impelled us to enter into this contract. We thought last year that it was proper to estimate that $40,000 would build the mountain section. WTe came to this conclusion after the best consideration we could give to the matter. I do not know that at that time our figures were seriously challenged, but we were bound to assume that the Grand Trunk estimate, as stated by the president, would be some $50,000. That was the information we had put before us. If it were $40,000, as we anticipated, then our liability would remain at $30,000 per mile. If it were more, as was the estimate of the president of the Grand Trunk Company at the meeting of the shareholders when he said that it would be $50,000 a mile, then our liability would increase according to ratio to $37,000 a mile. But, how much it will be is a contingent question which cannot be decided at this moment. It is not easy to speculate upon this ; it is not easy to enter into an argument upon it. We assume that it must be between these two figures and we think it will remain at $40,000 a mile. There are some portions of the mountain section which are very difficult of construction, but we know that in the lower portion of the Pine River valley it is not difficult work. It will be very much like the prairie section, but taking it all in all, we have no reason to change our estimate of last year that it will not go beyond $40,000 a mile. But, since I am upon this question I would like to call the attention of my hon. friend from Hamilton to a speech which he has made and repeated several times as to what would be the cost of this road which he has estimated at $56,000 a mile. I may perhaps read his remarks. Speaking of the president of the Grand Trunk Railway Company he said :
Well, that gentleman told his shareholders that the cost of the mountain section would be $50,000 per mile, to which he added, as an item of cost, three years' Interest at four per cent, making up the ieost of construction of the mountain section to $56,000 per mile.
That is a matter that I understand always goes with the construction of the road. You do not charge for interest on $40,000, $50,000 or $60,000 per mile but you Include everything in the cost, including interest. If he has put the cost at $50,000 a mile I imagine that $50,000 would include also the interest.
Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson expressly adds interest to the $50,000 a mile.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It does not make $56,000 a mile.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If Mr. Hays has the right to charge interest on the cost of construction I do not anticipate and I never understood that he would charge in addition to the $50,000 per mile. But, Mr. Hays has no right to calculate it at four per cent. The contract says that he may pay four per cent or ten per cent for his money but all he can charge against the road is three per cent and no more on account of the cost of construction. Whereas my hon. friend in his speech calculated it at four per cent. I think my hon. friend made a mistake and that on careful consideration he would be bound to revise his figures.
If I understood the right hon. gentleman correctly he says that he understands that Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson is not adding interest during construction to the $50,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He may. But, for my part, as I understand these questions, in calculating the cost of construction, whether it be $40,000, or $50,000, or $60,000 per mile, or any amount, the interest always goes into the total. Interest may go on from time to time and whoever constructs the road has to charge interest from year to year, and certainly when we calculated that $40,000 a mile would be the cost of construction we included interest at three per cent per annum.

There is no doubt about what the right hon. gentleman says that when you find out first of all precisely the number of dollars per mile you pay your contractor, say, $50,000 a mile, you then, in order to ascertain the cost of construction, have to add to that $50,000 a mile what you have to pay your banker for the loan of the money you pay out to your contractor before the line begins to earn anything. On a line taking six years to construct the average interest period would be about three years, and whatever interest you would have to pay to your banker in addition to what you pay your contractor is properly chargeable to construction. So that. Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson in stating to his shareholders what the line is going to cost them puts the construction cost at $50,000 and then he adds interest during construction.

Let

me say this. One of the greatest objections I have to this scheme is that, if this road should not pay, the government has absolutely no security that they will be reimbursed the interest. They have provided, it is true, that if the road goes into default, it shall be managed by a receiver, and, that three-quarters of the earnings shall go to the government and one-quarter to the Grand Trunk Pacific. The bargain gives the Grand Trunk Railway directors absolute control of this railway company. It provides that the Grand Trunk Railway shall hold control for all time. In other words, no matter how great may be the default or how long, the Grand Trunk Railway will nominate the directors and control the road. I thinkj that that, apart from the financial features of this scheme, is the weakest part of the whole thing. The Grand Trunk Railway, under this agreement, own absolutely the Grand Trunk Pacific. In case of default by the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Grand Trunk Railway will still have absolute control of the directors of the defaulting company. They will elect them all, without the government having any voice or say in the matter ; and assuming default, what is more likely than that the court will say that the Grand Trunk Railway, having control of the directors, shall have the nomination of their receiver. That goes without saying. I should hope that before we get through this Bill, the government will put in a clause providing that, in case of default, the whole Grand Trunk Pacific shall be handed over to the government to be controlled by the government, so that the government may elect the directors of the Grand Trunk Pacific so long as that company is in default one dollar. If you do that, you would practically control the company ; but if the company gets into default, and the Grand Trunk Pacific have control, then the Grand Trunk Railway dominates the policy of that company. It will dominate the appointment of a receiver.

If we are to implement the amount by making up the difference in one form or another we must have an assurance that these bonds are to be sold for a fair and reasonable price. If they were placed at a low price, then we would have an additional sum to make up in Out form or another over and above that which we might fairly expect, and if we did not have some such provision in regard to these bonds, I think my hon. friend would be the first to say that there would be danger in a business transaction like this. We are bound to look on all sides of it. It would be quite possible for the company to enter into arrangements for the floating of these bonds, which might not be wise or prudent. The flotation might be made upon extravagant terms which might involve large commissions and profits, and viewed in this light, we think that there should be some method by which it can be determined whether the bonds that (he company are issuing, are realizing a fair price or not. The clause reads in this way :
The terms and conditions upon which the bonds to be guaranteed by the government pursuant to the said agreement in aid of the construction of the western division of the railway referred to therein or any portion of them, may he sold, pledged or otherwise disposed of by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, shall be subject to the approval of the Minister of Finance and Receiver General and of the Governor in Council.
Now the weakness of this, as it strikes me, is that during the construction of the railway, which will extend over a considerable period of time, the Grand Trunk people may say : We have an offer for $10.-(*'<'0,000 of these bonds at ninety cents on the dollar. The government are then face to face with the proposition whether they will accept the offer or whether they will say : No, we will not accept it. If the government Mr. FIELDING.
do not accept the offer and the bonds are subsequently sold at a lesser price, the Grand Trunk Railway will naturally say to the government : We offered you ninety cents for these bonds and you would not accept it. You must therefore take the risk. I think that in dealing with these bonds the government should have absolute power without reference to the Grand Trunk Railway Company at all to sell them ; in other words, the proper method, to my mind, would be, assuming that this is carried, for the government to p*ay the Grand Trunk Railway Company the money as the work progresses, and then let the government take their own way of selling the bonds. If the government do not do that, they are open to complications all the time. A syndicate is formed and offers a price for these bonds, the government do not agree to it, and afterwards, when the price goes down, the company will come and say : We offered you this price and you must make up the difference.

I would like to ask in what position we would be if, owing to the action of the government, delay was brought about whereby these bonds sold at par or more than par. Would the Grand Trunk give us the difference ?

Under this clause the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company have it all their own way. If the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company submitted to the government an offer of ninety cents on the dollar for these bonds and the government did not take it and afterwards the bonds had to be sold at eighty cents, the government would lose the money and not the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company.

Eight years from the completion of the road and possibly ten on the mountain section.

Mr. HAG6AKT. Eight years after construction.

It has been stated a good many times with a great deal of emphasis, that this road is to be of the standard of the Grand Trunk Railway. That is simply an impossibility. The Grand Trunk Railway road has only reached its present standard after many years of work on the roadbed.
But it will he such a road that, in the course of time, it will arrive at the standard of the Grand Trunk Railway. You may buy an extra fine brand of port wine, but it will take time to mellow.

The contrast was drawn in favour of this against other contracts, That the standard of the Grand Trunk, which is to be the standard of this road, is so much higher than that of other companies, that have been aided by the government. But the Canadian Northern was to be a high class road, and we cannot build a road higher than a high class road in a new country. Before you can get this Grand Trunk Pacific or any road over the prairie or any where in this country up to the standard of the Grand Trunk Railway, you will have to expend ten or fifteen or twenty years perhaps in constant renewals and expenditure on the track and road-bed. It will cost $10,000 a mile at the very least, during the ten years after this road is constructed, to keep it in first-class condition and repair. That $10,000 will come out of the earnings of the company. The Grand Trunk Railway may spend any sum they please out of the earnings on that road, so that it will not pay. Then if there is any default in the payment of interest, it goes into the hands of a receiver, and the Grand Trunk Railway will have the control of the directors who will appoint the receiver.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Under section 114 of the Railway Act, the bondholders will control the directors.

In any event, no matter what may be earned, the Grand Trunk Railway, if they like may spend all the earnings on the main line to bring it to the standard of the Grand Trunk Railway.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Will my hon. friend the Minister of Justice explain the effect of these sections ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Under the original agreement, in the event of default on the part of the company, the power of foreclosure and sale would be vested, under ordinary circumstances, in the government. This provides that, in the event of default, before any proceeding by way of foreclosure and sale can take place, the default must continue for a period of five years. I should say there instead of the ordinary proceeding by way of foreclosure, a manager or receiver will be appointed, who will take charge of the road and oper-it, and he shall account for the proceeds in the proportion of three-fourths to the government and one-fourth to the bondholder. The effect, in so far as the bondholders are concerned, is that instead of putting the holders of the second issue of bonds, that is, the issue guaranteed by the Grand Trunk, in the position of losing the whole of their investment in the Grand Trunk Pacific in case of default and| the road passing into the hands of the govern^ ment, the holders of the second issue of bonds will be in the same position in effect as the holders of the first issue with respect to the revenue of the road, in case of the

default of the Grand Trunk Pacific. There are three departures from the original contract. The first is that a foreclosure and sale cannot take place ; the road is to be operated for five years before proceedings by way of foreclosure can be taken at all. Then after that the foreclosure proceedings are not the ordinary ones of our own statute, but are of a modified form, an entry into possession by the government through a manager, which manager will operate the road for the joint benefit of all the bondholders. That is to say the government will get 75 per cent of the profits of the road and the holders of the second issue of bonds will get 25 per cent.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The position of a mortgagee in possession is not a very desirable one. I think a mortgagee in possession is almost the only individual against whom accounts are taken in the first instance on the footing of wilful default, and it does not seem to me to be very much in the public interest that the country should be placed in that position. The Minister of Justice says there is a change in the method of foreclosure ; I do not see there is any foreclosure at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As a matter of fact there is not; it is a modified form of entering into possession.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Simply a form of entering into possession, and as I said the position of a mortgagee in possession is not a desirable one because unless it is modified by the terms of this contract-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: By the very last paragraph of clause 7.

BORDEN (reading)
The said manager or agent is to be appointed by the government, with the concurrence of the company, or, if they are unable to agree, by a majority of the Supreme Court of Canada.
I have not considered the matter carefully from this standpoint because the suggestion I have made only entered my mind at the moment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That was a suggestion that entered our minds at the time.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
What is the reason that the title of this road is to be kept in the company for ever, although they may be in default for ever ? Why should you so greatly modify the terms of a mortgage of this character ? For example we have had placed on the table of the House the mortgage by which the government is indemnified in respect of its bond guarantee for the Canadian Northern Railway Company and I find that that mortgage is enforceable under certain conditions. One of these conditions is that if the company make default for a period of six calendar months in the Mr. FITZPATRICK.
payment of interest the government can enter, can sell, and convey and give title. If it does not desire to exercise the powers of sale conferred on it, it can under section 3 of the mortgage, proceed by way of ordinary foreclosure and obtain title in the same way. Here, you have an absolutely different scheme. A scheme such as that contained in the Canadian Northern mortgage, is infinitely more in the interests of the country and why is the country asked to submit to a scheme under which the government cannot take possession unless the interest is in arrears for five years and even if that default arises the government cannot foreclose or obtain a title. The differences are very marked between this mortgage and that of the Canadian Northern which I am using as an illustration because that mortgage is in the ordinary form. Under the ordinary mortgage you can proceed upon default of six month's interest. As soon as ti months' interest are in default you can proceed with all your remedies under the mortgage. Then there is the further marked difference that whereas under the ordinary mortgage you can proceed to foreclose to make title and to acquire the interest of the mortgagor in the railway, you cannot under this do anything of the kind so far as I understand. These are changes of the most extreme, radical type and I would ask some explanation of the government as to why what seem to me to be most remarkable, most unusual and unheard of provisions should be contained in the supplementary agreement, especially when every line of the original agreement had been assented to by the gentlemen concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The conditions in the Canadian Northern mortgage are the usual ones. My hon. friend would understand that there is a broad line of demarcation between the Canadian Northern securities and .these now being considered. In the case of the Canadian Northern, we are dealing with a company the bonds of which we guaranteed purely and simply. We take such mortgages as a creditor under similar conditions would take as security. In the present ease we are dealing with the Grand Trunk Pacific Company and also with the Grand Trunk Railway Company. It must be borne in mind that the first issue of bonds is by the Grand Trunk Pacific Company. That issue is guaranteed by the government, and that issue, in so far as the contract applies, will only procure three-fourths of the cost of the construction of the road. It is therefore necessary to have in addition to that provision for the other one quarter. Parliament has chosen to approve the action of the government in saying that the Grand Trunk Railway Company should guarantee the second issue. In the event of foreclosure, under ordinary cir-

cum stances and. under the original contract, the second issue of bonds would be wiped out, and the Grand Trunk Railway Company as endorsers would become liable to the bondholders but would have no claim whatever upon the road. The Grand Trunk Company endorse the second issue, and thus became liable to the holders of the bonds. Then being simply the holders of the second mortgage they would be absolutely without any recourse except against the Grand Trunk. Under these circumstances we suggested that the Grand Trunk Company should guarantee the second issue of bonds in the same way as the government guaranteed the first issue as it is their credit that will enable the Grand Trunk Pacific Company to float the second issue of bonds just as it was the credit of the government that enabled the company to float the first issue of bonds. There was no reason why, in case of default, the road should pass from their hands and not be administered for the benefit of both endorsers. That was the position they took and there is something in it. The change is made to put the endorsers, the Grand Trunk Railway Company in the same position as the guarantors of the first issue. We hear a good deal about the prairie section and the mountain section. W e have been told that the prairie section is to pay and if there is any doubt as to the western section not all paying it is m regard to the mountain section If there is any default the whole road goes, the prairie section as well as the mountain section.
Goes where ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Into the hands of the manager. It must be borne in mind that the company will take care of the fat section. We are here making provision for a contingency which can never possiblv occur. The company will never allow the' prairie section to pass out of their hands. They will make their arrangements and they will see to it that the road is managed in such a way that we will never be called upon to enter into possession. A fact which is not to be lost sight of, is that the prairie section is bound up with the mountain section in such a way that if they default on the mountain section the prairie section goes u ith it. The position that the government took was a fair one. We have confidence in this country and we have confidence in the country that will be served by this road. All that we are doing is to facilitate the financing of this enterprise by giving to these people the means necessary to enable them to build this road at a cheap figure: Instead of being obliged to go out into the money market and offer their bonds, taking what they can get for them, the government are lending their credit to the companv so that they will get their money at the lowest possible rate and get the road constructed as 78
cheaply as possible. We know the resources of that country, and we feel that we are absolutely safe in that respect. We know that the prairie section is possessed of an enormous amount of earning power and that section will be sufficient to make up any short-comings with respect to the mountain section. We know that the earning power of the prairie section must contribute to the maintenance of the mountain section. We are satisfied that all we are doing is to lend our credit to this company and that we will not be called upon to pay a farthing except our contribution in respect to interest. In doing that we give confidence to those timid English shareholders of the Grand Trunk Railway Company who appear not to know very much about this country. We say : we know this country is safe, we know that the people of this country have confidence in this enterprise and we will guarantee three-quarters of the c-ost-
Why not guarantee it all!

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I gave that answer to the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Osier) a little while ago. We know that eventually this country will be prosperous, that its resources are of such a magnitude that this enterprise will not involve anything as far as the country is concerned. We have said to these English shareholders : We do not hesitate to give you an assurance that these are our convictions and as a result some of the timidity of the English shareholders has been brushed aside and they now; see it in a different light. Not only have we told them that we are prepared to guarantee three-quarters of the cost of the construction, knowing that it involves no liability, but we say that we believe that the earning power will be such as to enable them to receive their interest upon their investment. But, in case our expectations are not realized and if, as a matter of fact, the predictions that have been made in other quarters are realized and under this clause the road should pass into the hands of a receiver we will put ourselves on the same footing as you are and we will agree to take three-quarters of the earning power of the road over and above the running expenses giving * you the other one quarter.

We are not on the same plane as the Grand Trunk Railway Company. Under this contract the government are not getting their fair share. You are giving the Grand Trunk Pacific not only their full share but you are giving them absolute control.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is entirely mistaken about that.

The government are giving the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company the right to build branches from this, the backbone of the road, to Lake Superior and they virtually have no control over them. If

And that belongs to

I would like to ask the hon. Minister of Justice a question I understand the hon. minister to say that the obiect of this clause is to postpone the right of foreclosure and sale until there has been five years default.

The ordinary provision is that if there is one coupon in arrear for five years or any period you can proceed.

speechtext: If there is one coupon in arrear for six months you can proceed.

The hon. gentleman says that this clause has been put in to'Prevent hardship. This provides that until they shall be five whole years in default, ten coupons in effect, you cannot take any steps. L there are nine coupons in arrear the government cannot stir.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

That is a very different thing from the ordinary procedure when there is default. It means that at any time during the forty years the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company can allow eight or-nine coupons to remain in default and if these coupons remain outstanding or rather have been paid by the government and the o-overnment hold them for forty years they cannot collect them. That is the position of this extraordinary contract.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

That would be mortgaged also, and the hon. gentleman knows that you cannot recover anything by suit from a railway company when it is all mortgaged up to the handle.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have collected dozens of times from railway companies.
I never heard of any such provision in a contract before. In case of default the Grand Trunk on its guarantee can take any proceeding it likes, but the government can take no step.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: What effect would that have with respect to us ?
I will tell you in a moment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Oh, tell it no\y.
I am asking questions at present.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: And you are evading mine. My hon. friend must not imagine that none of us have read a word of law If he reads section 114 of the Railway Act he will find his answer.

You have forced the Grand Trunk to control the Grand Trunk Pacific, and handling the cash from day to day, it can pay the interest upon the Grand Trunk guarantee, and leave the government guarantee in default.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In case the second bondholders take proceedings what becomes op the first bondholders ?
The government will take proceedings specified by this contract, and get an agent, but the Grand Trunk Railway will have a receiver who will be the Grand Trunk under another name.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I know my hon. friend's capacity in railway affairs, and he must know that under section 114 of the Railway Act the first bondholders become co-ad the company's shareholders, for the purpose of electing directors, and as we have three-fourths of the bonds, what becomes of the other one-fourth ?
In this contract the Minister of Justice has tied the country up, leaving the other bondholders free td every remedy the law gives them.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Not at all.

I doubt very much whether the hon. gentleman has ever seen a case where the first mortgage bondholders were precluded from their remedy, and the second mortgage bondholders were allowed to go on and get a receiver.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The first mortgage bondholders are not precluded. The law protects them.

Supposing the Grand Trunk Pacific under the dictation of the Grand Trunk Railway used the cash receipts they have in hand to pay the CQupons that the Grand Trunk Company guarantee; there is nothing here to prevent that. The result would be that there would be three years' default on the bonds guaranteed by the government and the government will have to pay the interest and capitalize it.

Before the hon. gentleman (Mr. Barker) sits down, probably he will answer a question I will put to him. Assuming that all the prognostications that have been made should turn out to be correct, and this road prove to be an absolute failure from beginning to end; in what worse position would we be, than if the views of our friends on the other side prevailed and we were to build the road as a government undertaking.
That is very fine reasoning.
Probably my hon. friend will answer that question.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I will answer the hon. gentleman. In a matter of this kind, we have to look at the possibilities both in the case of success and in the case of failure. We all hope that this enterprise will be a success. If it is a success, and if the views expressed from this side of the House should be given effect to, then we would have a road which would be a magnificent asset for the country, and we would be a great deal better off than we will be under this contract. If on the other hand, there is a failure, then we will be practically as badly off as we would be if we were to build the road ourselves. Let me point out that the Minister of Justice has given a very effective answer to the remarks made by the Minister of Customs this afternoon. The Minister of Justice says that the prairie section is so valuable an asset that it will more than offset any disadvantage in building the mountain section, and therefore the proposition as a whole will be a good one for this country to undertake.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Except, that I do not believe in government ownership.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: My hon. friend the Minister of Customs evidently does.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Chacun son gofit.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
If the Minister of Customs were present, I would refer him to the Minister of Justice for an answer to everything he urged this afternoon. Now, the Minister of Justice has introduced a matter which I proposed to introduce later, namely, the placing of the bonds guaranteed by the Grand Trunk upon equality with those guaranteed by the govern-

ment. That is a very good thing for the Grand Trunk and for the holders of the bonds guaranteed by the Grand Trunk ; but the very' fact that the government have put those bonds in that position is the best possible argument against introducing these other stipulations in the contract. When you have these bonds, there ought be no reason for postponing entry and foreclosure until five years' default has taken place. Why should there be any stipulation in the contract absolutely abolishing any foreclosure at all? The hon. gentleman refers by illustration to the mortgage given by the Canadian Northern for similar bonds guaranteed by the government. Well, ought the Canadian Northern be in any better position if it had created another company called the Canadian Northern Pacific Railway Company, obtained a government guarantee for the bonds of that company, and guaranteed one-fourth of the bonds itself. That is all the Grand Trunk has done. Why should the Grand Trunk be in any better position because, as was frankly stated at a meeting of its shareholders, it has created another corporation called the Grand Trunk Pacific for the purpose of carrying this enterprise out. The Minister of Justice says that that alters the situation, but it ought not to alter the situation. After all, the main feature of this is that the government undertake to guarantee bonds representing three-quarters of the cost of the road and the government did practically the same thing as far as the prairie section of the Canadian Northern is concerned.
In the one case the trustee acting for the government has the right to enter upon default in payment of one coupon representing interest for six months. In this case the Grand Trunk Railway Company can do what my hon. friend from Hamilton has said, and it can do more. It can designedly permit the first nine coupons to be defaulted, and to be paid by the government, and it can let these stand for the remaining period of fifty years ; and unless it has money to burn, to use a common expression, it will do that. Why is the government called upon to put the country in that position ? If six months' default is sufficient in the case of the Canadian Northern Railway mortgage, why is it not sufficient in the case of this mortgage ? The Minister of Justice suggests that to permit this default to continue makes the position of the government better, because it gives the company a better opportunity of carrying on its railway. Exactly the same considerations would apply in the case of the Canadian Northern or any other company whose bonds are guaranteed. You would put them in a better position the more you gave away to them. That is very plain ; but is it necessary for the country to give so much away simply fm the purpose of putting the company in Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
a better position ? As my hon. friend from Hamilton suggests, the four and a half years is in addition to the ten years. In the first place, you have the eight years during which the road is being constructed ; after that, so far as the mountain section is concerned, you have seven years during which the government assumes the interest ; after that you have the three years during which the interest cannot be enforced, but may be capitalized under certain conditions ; and after that you have the four and a half years during which the Grand Trunk Pacific may make default in payment of interest, and for the payment of that interest the government has no remedy whatever during the entire period of fifty years providing the remaining interest is paid as it becomes due.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think the hon. gentleman makes an exact statement when he says that we are without any remedy.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I admit that the mortgage may be so drawn as to give the government a right of action. It may enter up a judgment, but when it does, what can it do afterwards ? Can it take any effective proceedings ? It may issue an execution only to find every available asset of the Grand Trunk Pacific covered by some prior charge. Tt may sell subject to this prior charge ; but will that be an effective remedy ? Will the Minister of Justice say that you can get title under that ? It seems to me you could not. because you would have to face the prior charges of the bonds guaranteed by the government and those guaranteed by the Grand Trunk Railway Company. Therefore, after all. it is a mere visionary remedy, and will not result, so far as we can see. in any actual payment under the judgment. These are remarkable provisions, and I do not see why the government should be driven to make conditions of this kind when they were not considered necessary in a similar case last year. Why is it that the usual default should not give the government any remedy under this contract ? Why is it that what you call a mortgage is legislated out of being a mortgage and is constituted a mere charge under which the government can enter into possession and may be placed in a very unfortunate position by being called upon at some time to render an account of the receipts and profits of this road .' I must confess that the explanation of the Minister of Justice seems to me insufficient and inadequate. I cannot conceive of any possible ground which could have induced the government to enter into a contract of this kind. Section 7 of schedule agreed to.

surplus tolls and revenues shall have paid off all arrears of such Interest.
